docs.title: AI agent
docs.body:
# AI agent

An AI tool that does more than answer a question. Given a goal, it takes a series of steps on its own, such as looking things up, using other software and checking its own results. Builders often describe it as a model that uses tools in a loop.

Also called: agent, agents, agentic, autonomous agent.

**Example:** You ask an AI agent to find three venues for an event. It searches, compares prices, checks which dates are open and returns a shortlist.

# Prompt injection

A security weakness in AI products. Text that a model reads changes its behavior in ways the builder did not intend. The text can come from the user or hide in outside content such as a web page or a file.

Also called: prompt injections, prompt injection attack, indirect prompt injection, injection attack.

**Example:** An AI assistant summarizes a web page. Hidden text on the page tells it to send the user's saved notes to a stranger. Without defenses, the assistant may follow that text.

docs.title: Vibe coding vs software engineering
docs.body:
# Vibe coding vs software engineering

Two ways to build software with AI. In vibe coding, a term Andrej Karpathy coined in 2025, a person accepts the code the AI writes without reading it. In software engineering with AI help, a person reviews, tests and can explain the code. The programmer Simon Willison draws the line at that review.

Also called: writing code vs prompting, prompting vs coding, prompting code, AI-assisted programming, AI-assisted coding, AI-assisted engineering.

**Example:** A founder prompts an app builder until a demo works and never opens the code. That is vibe coding. An engineer uses a coding agent, reads each change and runs the tests before release. That is software engineering.

**Connected on the map to:** Vibe coding, Software engineer, Coding agent, Testing, Technical debt, Claude Code, Codex.

docs.title: Agent Skills (SKILL.md format)
docs.body:
# Agent Skills (SKILL.md format)

Agent Skills are an open format for packaging instructions and resources that an AI agent loads on demand.

- agentskills.io: "Agent Skills are a lightweight, open format for extending AI agent capabilities with specialized knowledge and workflows."
- A skill is a folder with a required `SKILL.md` file. Its frontmatter has at least `name` and `description`, followed by instructions. Optional folders: `scripts/`, `references/`, `assets/`.
- Progressive disclosure in three stages: Discovery (load only each skill's name and description at startup), Activation (read the full `SKILL.md` when a task matches), Execution (follow it, running bundled code or loading files as needed).
- This keeps many skills available with a small context footprint.
- The format was originally developed by Anthropic and released as an open standard; the site says a growing number of agent products have adopted it.
- [Google Antigravity](../products/google-antigravity.md)'s CLI carries over Agent Skills from [Gemini CLI](../products/gemini-cli.md). [GDG Tulsa](../orgs/gdg-tulsa.md) ran [a session on agent skills](../events/gdg-wordpress-put-agent-skills-to-work-2026-10-29.md) in October 2026. [Brainmaxxing](brainmaxxing.md) ships its loop as skills.

## Sources

- [Agent Skills overview](https://agentskills.io/)

docs.title: AGENTS.md
docs.body:
# AGENTS.md

AGENTS.md is an open Markdown file convention for giving coding agents project instructions, "a README for agents."

- Typical contents: setup and build commands, test instructions, code style, PR or commit rules, security notes and deployment steps. No sections are required.
- A README is for human contributors; AGENTS.md holds agent-focused detail that would clutter a README.
- Monorepos can put an AGENTS.md in each subproject. Agents read the nearest file in the directory tree, and explicit user prompts override all AGENTS.md files.
- The site says over 60k open-source projects use it (checked 2026-11-18).
- Supporting tools listed include OpenAI Codex, Google Jules, Cursor, Aider, goose, opencode, Zed, Warp, VS Code, Devin, JetBrains Junie, Amp, RooCode, [Gemini CLI](../products/gemini-cli.md), GitHub Copilot's coding agent, Windsurf and Augment Code.
- The format is now stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation.
- Related: Gemini CLI's own `GEMINI.md` context files, [Agent Skills](agent-skills.md), [Brainmaxxing](brainmaxxing.md).

## Sources

- [AGENTS.md](https://agents.md/)

docs.title: BM25 keyword ranking
docs.body:
# BM25 keyword ranking

BM25 (Okapi BM25) is a classic ranking function that scores documents by how well their words match a query.

- "BM" stands for "best matching." It treats documents as bags of words and ignores word order.
- It comes from the probabilistic retrieval framework developed in the 1970s and 1980s by Stephen E. Robertson, Karen Spärck Jones and others. "Okapi" was the system at City University, London, that first used it.
- Three ideas: term frequency (more matches score higher, with diminishing returns), inverse document frequency (rare words count more) and length normalization (long documents don't win just by being long).
- Free parameters: `k1` (typically 1.2 to 2.0) and `b` (typically 0.75).
- It is fast and good at exact terms like names and codes, but it does not know synonyms. Pair it with [embeddings](embeddings-and-semantic-search.md) in [hybrid search](hybrid-search.md).

## Sources

- [Okapi BM25 (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okapi_BM25)

docs.title: Brainmaxxing
docs.body:
# Brainmaxxing

Brainmaxxing is an open-source (MIT) Markdown memory vault and skill set that gives a coding agent persistent memory.

- Repo description: "stupid simple persistent memory and skill improvement." The README calls it "Stupid simple persistent memory for Claude Code."
- How it works: a Markdown vault (`brain/`) that the agent reads at session start and writes to when it learns something. It is also an Obsidian vault, so people can browse the agent's memory.
- Ships with 16 engineering principles as starter content and six skills. Four form a learning loop: `/reflect` (after a session, write lessons to the brain), `/ruminate` (mine past conversations), `/meditate` (audit and prune, improve skills). Two support work: `/plan` and `/review`.
- Two hooks inject the brain index at startup and rebuild it when files change.
- The README says "`/reflect` alone gets you most of the value."
- Install: copy `brain/`, `.agents/skills/`, `.claude/hooks/` and the brain instructions in `CLAUDE.md` into a project.
- Author: [Lauren Tan](../people/lauren-tan.md) (GitHub `poteto`); the repo was created in February 2026.
- Related: [Agent Skills](agent-skills.md), [AGENTS.md](agents-md.md).

## Sources

- [poteto/brainmaxxing (GitHub)](https://github.com/poteto/brainmaxxing)

docs.title: Embeddings and semantic search
docs.body:
# Embeddings and semantic search

An embedding turns text into a list of numbers so a computer can find passages with similar meaning, not just matching words.

- Hugging Face defines an embedding as "a numerical representation of a piece of information, for example, text, documents, images, audio, etc."
- A sentence can become a vector of, for example, 384 numbers. [all-MiniLM-L6-v2](../products/all-minilm-l6-v2.md) produces 384-dimension vectors.
- Semantic search: embed every document once, embed the query, score the query against each document, and return the closest.
- The Hugging Face guide uses cosine similarity by default; dot product is another option. With normalized vectors the two rank results the same way.
- [Transformers.js](../products/transformers-js.md) can compute embeddings in the browser, as [FetchMoji](fetchmoji-emoji-search.md) does.
- Embeddings can miss exact terms such as names or codes, which is why many systems add [BM25](bm25.md) keyword ranking and use [hybrid search](hybrid-search.md).

## Sources

- [Getting Started With Embeddings (Hugging Face, 2022)](https://huggingface.co/blog/getting-started-with-embeddings)
- [sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2](https://huggingface.co/sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2)

docs.title: FetchMoji (emoji-search)
docs.body:
# FetchMoji (emoji-search)

FetchMoji is an open-source emoji finder that runs semantic search entirely in the browser.

- README: "Find the perfect emoji using your own words. All ranking and inference run fully client‑side (No API Keys, no telemetry)." Site: fetchmoji.com. Repo: ThatGuySam/emoji-search.
- Stack: Astro + React, PGlite (Postgres in WASM) with pgvector in the browser, and [Transformers.js](../products/transformers-js.md) running the Xenova `gte-small` ONNX embedding model.
- Uses WebAssembly SIMD, threads when the page is cross-origin isolated, and WebGPU when available.
- The vector table is prebuilt and packed into a tarball that PGlite restores at runtime. Source data: about 3k core emoji plus curated synonyms and verb-to-emoji hints.
- Embedding work runs in a web worker off the main thread; the target is under 100 ms from keystroke to results. It works offline after first load.
- Shows the same idea as this brain's search: embed text once, then compare query vectors locally. See [Embeddings and semantic search](embeddings-and-semantic-search.md).

## Sources

- [ThatGuySam/emoji-search (GitHub)](https://github.com/ThatGuySam/emoji-search)

docs.title: Hybrid search
docs.body:
# Hybrid search

Hybrid search runs keyword search and vector search together and merges the results into one ranked list.

- Weaviate's guide: "Hybrid search is a technique that combines multiple search algorithms."
- Keyword side: [BM25](bm25.md) (or BM25F). Vector side: dense [embeddings](embeddings-and-semantic-search.md). Both run in parallel, then results are fused.
- Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) sums reciprocal ranks from each list, so a document ranked well in either list rises.
- Relative score fusion normalizes each list's scores to 0-1 before weighting and adding them (Weaviate's default since v1.24).
- An `alpha` weight sets the balance: near 0 favors keyword, near 1 favors vector, 0.5 is equal (Weaviate's default is 0.75).
- Why it helps: vectors understand meaning (the guide's example reads "catch" as fishing, not baseball), while keyword matching keeps exact terms like "Alaskan Pollock" in play.

## Sources

- [Hybrid Search Explained (Weaviate, Jan 27, 2025)](https://weaviate.io/blog/hybrid-search-explained)

docs.title: Transformers.js
docs.body:
# Transformers.js

Transformers.js is Hugging Face's JavaScript library for running pretrained ML models in the browser.

- The docs say: "Run 🤗 Transformers directly in your browser, with no need for a server!" It aims to match the Python `transformers` API.
- Models run through ONNX Runtime. In the browser the default is WASM on the CPU; `device: 'webgpu'` uses the GPU (the docs note WebGPU is still experimental in many browsers).
- `dtype` picks precision: `fp32` (default for WebGPU), `fp16`, `q8` (default for WASM) or `q4`.
- Install: `npm i @huggingface/transformers`. The `pipeline()` function bundles a model with pre- and post-processing.
- Embedding example from the Xenova/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 card: `pipeline('feature-extraction', 'Xenova/all-MiniLM-L6-v2')`, then call it with `{ pooling: 'mean', normalize: true }` to get 384-dimension vectors. See [all-MiniLM-L6-v2](all-minilm-l6-v2.md).
- Used by [FetchMoji](../notes/fetchmoji-emoji-search.md) for in-browser semantic search. Background: [Embeddings and semantic search](../notes/embeddings-and-semantic-search.md).

## Sources

- [Transformers.js docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers.js/index)

chunks.heading: Agent Skills (SKILL.md format)
chunks.text:
Agent Skills are an open format for packaging instructions and resources that an AI agent loads on demand.
agentskills.io: "Agent Skills are a lightweight, open format for extending AI agent capabilities with specialized knowledge and workflows."
A skill is a folder with a required SKILL.md file. Its frontmatter has at least name and description, followed by instructions. Optional folders: scripts/, references/, assets/.
Progressive disclosure in three stages: Discovery (load only each skill's name and description at startup), Activation (read the full SKILL.md when a task matches), Execution (follow it, running bundled code or loading files as needed).
This keeps many skills available with a small context footprint.
The format was originally developed by Anthropic and released as an open standard; the site says a growing number of agent products have adopted it.

chunks.heading: BM25 keyword ranking
chunks.text:
BM25 (Okapi BM25) is a classic ranking function that scores documents by how well their words match a query.
"BM" stands for "best matching." It treats documents as bags of words and ignores word order.
It comes from the probabilistic retrieval framework developed in the 1970s and 1980s by Stephen E. Robertson, Karen Spärck Jones and others. "Okapi" was the system at City University, London, that first used it.
Three ideas: term frequency (more matches score higher, with diminishing returns), inverse document frequency (rare words count more) and length normalization (long documents don't win just by being long).
Free parameters: k1 (typically 1.2 to 2.0) and b (typically 0.75).
It is fast and good at exact terms like names and codes, but it does not know synonyms. Pair it with embeddings in hybrid search.

chunks.heading: Embeddings and semantic search
chunks.text:
An embedding turns text into a list of numbers so a computer can find passages with similar meaning, not just matching words.
Hugging Face defines an embedding as "a numerical representation of a piece of information, for example, text, documents, images, audio, etc."
A sentence can become a vector of, for example, 384 numbers. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 produces 384-dimension vectors.
Semantic search: embed every document once, embed the query, score the query against each document, and return the closest.
The Hugging Face guide uses cosine similarity by default; dot product is another option. With normalized vectors the two rank results the same way.
Transformers.js can compute embeddings in the browser, as FetchMoji does.
Embeddings can miss exact terms such as names or codes, which is why many systems add BM25 keyword ranking and use hybrid search.

chunks.heading: FetchMoji (emoji-search)
chunks.text:
FetchMoji is an open-source emoji finder that runs semantic search entirely in the browser.
README: "Find the perfect emoji using your own words. All ranking and inference run fully client‑side (No API Keys, no telemetry)." Site: fetchmoji.com. Repo: ThatGuySam/emoji-search.
Stack: Astro + React, PGlite (Postgres in WASM) with pgvector in the browser, and Transformers.js running the Xenova gte-small ONNX embedding model.
Uses WebAssembly SIMD, threads when the page is cross-origin isolated, and WebGPU when available.
The vector table is prebuilt and packed into a tarball that PGlite restores at runtime. Source data: about 3k core emoji plus curated synonyms and verb-to-emoji hints.
Embedding work runs in a web worker off the main thread; the target is under 100 ms from keystroke to results. It works offline after first load.

chunks.heading: FetchMoji (emoji-search)
chunks.text: Shows the same idea as this brain's search: embed text once, then compare query vectors locally. See Embeddings and semantic search.

chunks.heading: Hybrid search
chunks.text:
Hybrid search runs keyword search and vector search together and merges the results into one ranked list.
Weaviate's guide: "Hybrid search is a technique that combines multiple search algorithms."
Keyword side: BM25 (or BM25F). Vector side: dense embeddings. Both run in parallel, then results are fused.
Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) sums reciprocal ranks from each list, so a document ranked well in either list rises.
Relative score fusion normalizes each list's scores to 0-1 before weighting and adding them (Weaviate's default since v1.24).
An alpha weight sets the balance: near 0 favors keyword, near 1 favors vector, 0.5 is equal (Weaviate's default is 0.75).
Why it helps: vectors understand meaning (the guide's example reads "catch" as fishing, not baseball), while keyword matching keeps exact terms like "Alaskan Pollock" in play.

chunks.heading: all-MiniLM-L6-v2
chunks.text:
all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is a small sentence-transformers embedding model for semantic search and clustering.
The model card says it "maps sentences & paragraphs to a 384 dimensional dense vector space."
"input text longer than 256 word pieces is truncated," so it suits sentences and short paragraphs.
Fine-tuned from nreimers/MiniLM-L6-H384-uncased on "a 1B sentence pairs dataset"; the card says the total "is above 1 billion sentences."
License: Apache-2.0. Intended uses: information retrieval, clustering and sentence similarity.
Xenova/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is a port with "ONNX weights to be compatible with Transformers.js," so it runs in the browser with Transformers.js.
Background: Embeddings and semantic search.

chunks.heading: Gemini API
chunks.text:
The Gemini API is Google's developer API for Gemini models and managed agents.
The docs landing page ("Welcome to Gemini API") says: "Go from a quick prompt to production apps and agents with the Gemini API." The old ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs URL now redirects to aistudio.google.com/docs (checked 2026-11-18).
SDKs and interfaces shown: Python, JavaScript, REST, Java, Go and a CLI.
Models named on the page as of 2026-11-18 include Gemini 4 Carbon (gemini-4-carbon, 1M-token context), Gemini 4 Hydrogen (gemini-4-hydrogen), Gemini Decision 1, Gemini 3.8 Flash TTS and Nano Banana 2.1 (image generation). Model names change often.
API keys are created in Google AI Studio (aistudio.google.com/apikey). The REST example reads GEMINIAPIKEY and sends it in the x-goog-api-key header.

chunks.heading: Gemini API
chunks.text:
The page says "the Interactions API has become our default interface as of June 2026" and "the generateContent API is now considered legacy." The Python quickstart calls client.interactions.create().
Open-weight alternative: Gemma.

chunks.heading: Gemini (app)
chunks.text:
The Gemini app is Google's consumer AI assistant on web and mobile.
Google's overview page describes Gemini as "an interface to a multimodal LLM (handling text, audio, images and more)," with "mobile and web experiences."
Uses named on the page: summarizing long documents, help with coding, drafting outlines, generating images and explaining complex concepts.
The page mentions Gems, which let users customize Gemini with specific instructions. (checked 2026-11-18)
For developers, the same models are available through the Gemini API and Google AI Studio.

chunks.heading: Gemini CLI
chunks.text:
Gemini CLI is Google's open-source (Apache-2.0) terminal AI agent, now aimed at enterprise Gemini Code Assist users.
Repo description: "An open-source AI agent that brings the power of Gemini directly into your terminal." Install with npx @google/gemini-cli or npm install -g @google/gemini-cli.
Status change (as of 2026-11-18): the README says free individual access and Google AI Pro / Ultra moved to Antigravity CLI on June 18, 2026. Gemini CLI remains for Gemini Code Assist Standard / Enterprise, Code Assist for GitHub, and paid API keys. See Google Antigravity.
GEMINI.md context files: the docs say context files "use the default name GEMINI.md" and give the model project instructions, personas or style guides, so you don't repeat them in every prompt.

chunks.heading: Gemini CLI
chunks.text:
Load order: a global ~/.gemini/GEMINI.md, then GEMINI.md files in workspace directories and their parents, then "just-in-time" files found when a tool touches a directory. Contents are concatenated and sent with every prompt.
/memory show prints the combined context; /memory reload re-scans. Large files can import others with @file.md syntax.
The agents.md site lists Gemini CLI among tools that support AGENTS.md.

chunks.heading: Gemma
chunks.text:
Gemma is Google DeepMind's family of open models.
Google DeepMind calls them "Our most capable open models," built to run "from cloud servers to laptops and even phones."
Latest generation as of 2026-11-18: Gemma 4 (introduced April 2026), in E2B and E4B sizes for mobile and IoT, and 12B, 26B and 31B sizes for personal computers.
Related releases listed: Gemma 4 QAT, DiffusionGemma, EmbeddingGemma 2 and MedGemma 1.5 4B.
Available through Kaggle, Hugging Face, Ollama, Keras, PyTorch, Gemma.cpp, JAX, Google AI Edge, Google Cloud, Android AI Core, LM Studio and Unsloth. Gemma 4 31B can be tried in Google AI Studio.
The ai.google.dev/gemma URL now redirects to the DeepMind page.

chunks.heading: Google AI Studio
chunks.text:
Google AI Studio is Google's web workspace for trying Gemini models, getting API keys and building apps from prompts.
It is where developers create Gemini API keys (aistudio.google.com/apikey), and it now hosts the Gemini API docs.
Build mode: the docs say "AI Studio Build is a platform designed to take you from a simple prompt" to a working Gemini-powered app.
Default web stack: "A web frontend (React is the default)" plus "A Node.js runtime that allows for secure API calls." For Android it "generates a Kotlin and Jetpack Compose project."
"AI Studio automatically configures your Gemini API key as a secret in the app's server-side environment," so the key stays out of client code.
Ship options: deploy to Cloud Run, sync to a new or existing GitHub repository, or download a ZIP (then set GEMINIAPIKEY where you host it).

chunks.heading: Google AI Studio

chunks.text:

Platforms listed: macOS, Windows, Linux and Googlebook, plus a web app. For individual developers the site says "Available at no charge."

chunks.heading: Google Antigravity
chunks.text:
A Google Developers Blog post dated May 19, 2026 announced that Gemini CLI is transitioning to Antigravity CLI, which is "built in Go" and shares an agent harness with the Antigravity 2.0 desktop app. Agent Skills, Hooks, Subagents and Extensions (now "Antigravity plugins") carry over.
The Antigravity Agent harness also powers Google AI Studio Build mode.
Related: Agent Skills, Google for Developers.

chunks.heading: Transformers.js
chunks.text:
Transformers.js is Hugging Face's JavaScript library for running pretrained ML models in the browser.
The docs say: "Run 🤗 Transformers directly in your browser, with no need for a server!" It aims to match the Python transformers API.
Models run through ONNX Runtime. In the browser the default is WASM on the CPU; device: 'webgpu' uses the GPU (the docs note WebGPU is still experimental in many browsers).
dtype picks precision: fp32 (default for WebGPU), fp16, q8 (default for WASM) or q4.
Install: npm i @huggingface/transformers. The pipeline() function bundles a model with pre- and post-processing.
Embedding example from the Xenova/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 card: pipeline('feature-extraction', 'Xenova/all-MiniLM-L6-v2'), then call it with { pooling: 'mean', normalize: true } to get 384-dimension vectors. See all-MiniLM-L6-v2.
